instagram_caption:
What if you jumped into a tunnel straight through the Earth? 🌍⬇️

Say you dig it from Sydney, straight through the centre, and take out the air, the walls and Earth's spin. You'd fall through the crust, about 30–35 km thick under the continents, then 2,900 km of slowly flowing mantle, then liquid iron in the outer core, then the inner core, around 5,200–6,000 °C, roughly as hot as the Sun's surface.

Gravity gets a little stronger for the first 2,900 km down, so you keep speeding up. You'd reach the centre after about 19 minutes, doing about 36,000 km/h, and feel completely weightless. Then you'd slow down all the way up the other side and pop out of the North Atlantic, about 480 km southwest of the Azores, roughly 38 minutes after you jumped. Then you'd fall back in. Forever.

Reality check: the deepest hole humans have ever dug is the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia, 12,262 m deep by 1989. That's about 0.2% of the way to the centre. They stopped when the rock hit about 180 °C.

This is fiction. In reality, air and Earth's spin would stop you long before the core.

Would you jump? Did you spot him? 👀
